title: Sequential colimits represent homotopy colimits
statement: Let $\mathcal C$ be a site [def-weil-pbc-sites-and-cohomology], and let $\mathcal A=\Ab(\mathcal C)$, or let $\mathcal O$ be a sheaf of commutative rings on $\mathcal C$ and $\mathcal A=\Mod(\mathcal O)$ [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category]. Let $E_0^\bullet\xrightarrow{f_0}E_1^\bullet\xrightarrow{f_1}\cdots$ be a sequence of cochain complexes in $\mathcal A$, and write $Q:\mathrm{CoCh}(\mathcal A)\to D(\mathcal A)$ for localization [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. Put $A^\bullet=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}E_n^\bullet$ (degreewise coproduct), and define $u:A^\bullet\to A^\bullet$ by $u\iota_n=\iota_n-\iota_{n+1}f_n$. Let $L^\bullet=\varinjlim_n E_n^\bullet$ be the degreewise colimit [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit], with $q:A^\bullet\to L^\bullet$ induced by its structure maps. Then the canonical chain map $p:\operatorname{Cone}(u)\to L^\bullet$, equal to $q$ on $A^\bullet$ and zero on the shifted summand $A^\bullet[1]$, is a quasi-isomorphism. Moreover $Q(A^\bullet)$ with maps $Q(\iota_n)$ is the coproduct of $Q(E_n^\bullet)$ in $D(\mathcal A)$, and its cone triangle exhibits $Q(\operatorname{Cone}(u))$ as a homotopy colimit of that sequence [def-kun-truncations]. The isomorphism $Q(p)$ identifies this homotopy colimit with $Q(L^\bullet)$; transporting the cone triangle along $Q(p)$ exhibits $Q(L^\bullet)$ itself as a homotopy colimit. This includes the small etale site with any constant commutative coefficient ring, in particular $\mathbf Z/n$. No boundedness or monicity of the $f_n$ is required.

proof.text: Work throughout in the coefficient category $\mathcal A$ of the statement. For $\Ab(\mathcal C)$, small sequential colimits exist and are exact by the filtered-colimits theorem. For $\Mod(\mathcal O)$, the module-colimits theorem gives an abelian category, a faithful exact forgetful functor $U$ to $\Ab(\mathcal C)$, and existence of small colimits with $U(\varinjlim M_n)=\varinjlim U(M_n)$. Thus taking the underlying abelian sheaves of the colimit of a sequential diagram of short exact module sequences gives an exact sequence. This reflects exactness: $U$ preserves kernels and cokernels, so it preserves the homology object of a three-term sequence, and $U(H)=0$ implies $1_H=0$ by faithfulness. Kernels and cokernels detect the endpoint monicity and epicity in the same way. Hence sequential colimits are exact in either coefficient category. This is not an identification of their derived categories.

For $m\ge0$ form $B_m=\bigoplus_{n<m}E_n^\bullet$ and $C_m=\bigoplus_{n\le m}E_n^\bullet$. Map $v_m:B_m\to C_m$ by $\iota_n-\iota_{n+1}f_n$, and map $q_m:C_m\to E_m^\bullet$ by the sum of the transition maps $f_{n,m}$. The sequence $0\to B_m\xrightarrow{v_m}C_m\xrightarrow{q_m}E_m^\bullet\to0$ is split exact as complexes. Here $f_{n,m}=f_{m-1}\cdots f_n$ for $n<m$ and $f_{m,m}=1$. Indeed $q_m v_m=0$ since $f_{n,m}=f_{n+1,m}f_n$, and $q_m$ has the last-summand section. If $v_m(x)=0$, its first coordinate gives $x_0=0$ and its subsequent coordinates give $x_n=f_{n-1}x_{n-1}=0$, so $v_m$ is monic; for a tuple $y$ in $\ker(q_m)$ set $x_0=y_0$ and $x_n=y_n+f_{n-1}x_{n-1}$ for $n<m$. Then $v_m(x)=y$: the last equation is $y_m=-f_{m-1}x_{m-1}$, precisely $q_m(y)=0$. These finite matrix formulas are morphisms in $\mathcal A$ and commute with differentials. For $m=0$ this is $0\to0\to E_0\xrightarrow{1}E_0\to0$.

proof.text: The inclusions $B_m\to B_{m+1}$ and $C_m\to C_{m+1}$, together with $f_m:E_m\to E_{m+1}$, make these short exact sequences a sequential diagram: on the $n$-th summand both composites to $E_{m+1}$ are $f_{n,m+1}$. Its index $\mathbf N$ is small and filtered. Apply the exactness of sequential colimits in $\mathcal A$ established in step 1 separately in every cochain degree. Both colimits of finite sums are $A$: a compatible family of maps out of the finite sums is exactly a family of maps out of all $E_n$. Thus the colimit sequence is $0\to A\xrightarrow{u}A\xrightarrow{q}L\to0$, exact degreewise. The identifications commute with the differentials since all injections and transition maps are chain maps.

proof.text: The colimit relation $q\iota_{n+1}f_n=q\iota_n$ gives $qu=0$. In degree $r$, with the cone convention $\operatorname{Cone}(u)^r=A^r\oplus A^{r+1}$ and $d(b,a)=(db+ua,-da)$, the map $p^r(b,a)=q^r(b)$ satisfies $p^{r+1}d(b,a)=dq^r(b)$ because $qu=0$. This constructs exactly the asserted canonical chain map, without choosing an isomorphism of triangulated cones.

Apply the canonical cone projection theorem to the short exact sequence of complexes from step 3, in the abelian category $\mathcal A$. It asserts that the map from $\operatorname{Cone}(u)$ to $L$, equal to $q$ on the unshifted summand and zero on the shifted summand, is a quasi-isomorphism. Its two restrictions identify it with the map $p$ constructed in step 4, giving the conclusion.

Countable sums in $\mathcal A$ are exact. Indeed, for any countable family of short exact sequences take its finite initial sums: these are short exact because finite biproducts preserve kernels and cokernels coordinatewise. Their sequential colimit is the countable-sum sequence: maps out of the finite initial sums compatible with inclusions are exactly families of maps from the summands. Exact sequential colimits from step 1 therefore give exactness of that sequence. A finite or empty family is handled by its finite biproduct, and an arbitrary infinite countable family is reindexed by $\mathbf N$. Apply [lem-kun-derived-countable-sums-exact] to $(E_n^\bullet)$ in $\mathcal A$. Its exact-countable-sums hypothesis has just been verified, so $Q(A^\bullet)$ with the actual maps $Q(\iota_n)$ is the coproduct of the $Q(E_n^\bullet)$ in $D(\mathcal A)$, without a boundedness hypothesis.

By the cone-triangle convention, $Q(A)\xrightarrow{Q(u)}Q(A)\to Q(\operatorname{Cone}(u))\to Q(A)[1]$ is distinguished. Step 6 supplies its two genuine derived coproducts. Additivity of $Q$ and the defining equations on each coprojection give $Q(u)Q(\iota_n)=Q(\iota_n)-Q(\iota_{n+1})Q(f_n)$, so its first map is exactly $1-\operatorname{shift}$ in the definition of homotopy colimit. This triangle therefore exhibits $Q(\operatorname{Cone}(u))$ as a homotopy colimit. Step 5 makes $Q(p)$ an isomorphism. Replace the third vertex by $Q(L)$, compose the second arrow with $Q(p)$, and precompose the last arrow with $Q(p)^{-1}$: the resulting triangle is isomorphic to the cone triangle and hence distinguished. Its second arrow is $Q(q)$ because $p$ restricted to the cone inclusion is $q$. Thus $Q(L)$ is a homotopy colimit with its actual structure maps. All calculations were performed in $\mathcal A$, so the module case follows within $D(\Mod(\mathcal O))$, including constant coefficients on the small etale site. The assertion makes no canonical-isomorphism claim for an arbitrary separately chosen triangulated cone.
